name: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas

reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A rare epithelial neoplasm of low malignant potential that arises predominantly in young women
Often presents as a large, well-circumscribed mass with mixed solid and cystic components, sometimes with haemorrhage or a fibrous capsule
Frequently asymptomatic or causes vague abdominal discomfort, and may be found after minor trauma to a bulky lesion
Immunohistochemistry typically shows nuclear beta-catenin staining reflecting an underlying CTNNB1 mutation, along with markers such as CD10 and progesterone receptor
Imaging shows an encapsulated lesion with heterogeneous internal architecture and areas of degeneration; calcification may be present
The mainstay of treatment is complete surgical resection, which is curative in the great majority of cases
Even lesions with local invasion or limited metastases can have a favourable outcome after resection, reflecting the indolent biology
reference.pathophysiology: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasms are uncommon tumours of uncertain cell lineage that are strongly linked to activating mutations of the CTNNB1 gene and consequent abnormal Wnt/beta-catenin signalling, demonstrable as aberrant nuclear beta-catenin accumulation. The neoplastic cells are poorly cohesive and tend to fall away from delicate fibrovascular cores, creating the characteristic pseudopapillary pattern, while areas of the tumour undergo cystic degeneration and haemorrhage, producing the typical mixed solid and cystic mass. The marked female predominance and hormone-receptor expression suggest a hormonal influence on growth. Malignant potential is low, but a minority show local invasion or metastasis, most often to the liver or peritoneum.
additionalDifferentials: Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the pancreas
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to define the encapsulated solid-cystic mass and haemorrhagic components
Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle biopsy for tissue diagnosis
Immunohistochemistry including beta-catenin, CD10, and progesterone receptor
Cyst or lesion fluid analysis when cystic degeneration predominates
Staging imaging to assess for hepatic or peritoneal spread
Serum tumour markers (usually normal) to help exclude other diagnoses
redFlags: Local invasion of adjacent organs or vessels on imaging
Rapid growth or rupture with haemorrhage
Older or male patients or atypical histology, which may portend more aggressive behaviour
reference.prognosis: Overall prognosis is very good, with high cure rates after complete resection even for large tumours; a small proportion recur or metastasise, but survival remains favourable, and resection of limited metastatic disease is often worthwhile.
pitfalls: Mistaking the mass for a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour or adenocarcinoma and misdirecting treatment
Assuming benignity and forgoing resection, given the recognised though low malignant potential
Overlooking the diagnosis in the rare male or older patient because of the female predominance
Incomplete excision leaving a positive margin in a curable tumour
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
WHO classification of tumours of the digestive system
Reviews of solid pseudopapillary neoplasm outcomes and management
management: Complete surgical resection is the mainstay and is curative in the great majority, with the procedure such as enucleation, distal pancreatectomy or pancreaticoduodenectomy chosen by tumour location and spleen preservation where feasible.
Resection of limited hepatic or peritoneal metastatic disease is often worthwhile given the indolent behaviour.
Perioperative supportive care with pancreatic enzyme replacement and monitoring for diabetes where resection affects pancreatic function.
Chemotherapy and radiotherapy have only a limited role, reserved for rare unresectable or aggressive disease.
Postoperative surveillance imaging for the small risk of late recurrence or metastasis.
Manage through a hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgical multidisciplinary team.
